name: Liothyronine (T3)

lead: Liothyronine is lab-made T3, the active thyroid hormone, prescribed for hypothyroidism and in some thyroid cancer care. Some physique communities use it off-label for fat loss, and one looksmax.org thread claims it reduces eye puffiness.
Trials cover thyroid, depression and heart conditions, not fat loss or looks in healthy people.

paras: T3 enters cells and binds thyroid receptors in the nucleus, changing gene transcription and raising the body's metabolic activity. In people with normal thyroid function, supplemental hormone suppresses their own thyroid output.

The label's boxed warning says it should not be used for obesity or weight loss and that large doses may be life-threatening. Overdose causes hyperthyroid symptoms, heart rhythm problems and bone effects. It is prescription-only in the US.

lead: Liothyronine is the synthetic form of triiodothyronine (T3), the active thyroid hormone, sold in the United States as Cytomel and as generics. It is approved to treat hypothyroidism, to suppress thyroid-stimulating hormone as an adjunct in thyroid cancer care, and in thyroid suppression testing [1].

In bodybuilding and cutting culture, T3 has been used off-label by people without thyroid disease to raise metabolic rate and lose fat. A looksmax.org thread also describes a user who credits T3 pills with reducing puffiness around the eyes [2]. The FDA label carries a boxed warning that thyroid hormones should not be used for obesity or weight loss, stating that in euthyroid patients doses within the usual replacement range are ineffective for weight reduction and that larger doses may produce serious or life-threatening toxicity [1].

Controlled trials of liothyronine concern hypothyroidism, depression augmentation, heart disease and other medical conditions [3][4][5][6]. No trial found here tests it for fat loss or appearance in healthy people.
infobox: Hypothyroidism, TSH suppression in thyroid cancer care, diagnostic testing [1]
Boxed warning: not for obesity or weight loss [1]

paras: The usual treatment for hypothyroidism is levothyroxine (T4) [7][8]. Liothyronine is used in some patients and in combination with levothyroxine, an approach examined in several trials and covered by European and American guidelines [9][8]. Early trials found that adding T3 to T4 did not improve wellbeing, quality of life or cognition [10][11], while later studies compared levothyroxine, desiccated thyroid and combination therapy [3], and tested combination regimens in thyroidectomised patients [4][12]. Liothyronine has also been tested as an augmentation for antidepressant-resistant depression [5][13][14][15], and in heart failure and cardiac surgery settings [16][6][17].

Posts on looksmax.org describe taking T3 to reduce periorbital puffiness. One thread shows before-and-after images after three days of use and says the user expects results to normalise over three months; asked whether it must be taken for life, the original poster answers no [2]. Fat-loss use is mentioned in the wider cutting community, and the manufacturer label addresses it directly in a boxed warning [1].

Randomized trials in patients with hypothyroidism have compared T4 alone with T4 plus T3 [10][11][4][12][18] and with desiccated thyroid extract [3]. A phase 3 trial gave T3 to infants after cardiopulmonary bypass [17], and other studies examined T3 in insulin receptor mutations [19][20] and, as a topical product, diabetic foot ulcers [21]. These do not address fat loss or appearance in euthyroid individuals, and the label states that replacement-range doses are ineffective for weight reduction in euthyroid patients [1].

The label says adverse reactions are mainly those of hyperthyroidism from overdose: fatigue, increased appetite, weight loss, heat intolerance, sweating, headache, hyperactivity and nervousness, with cardiac adverse reactions including atrial fibrillation especially in older people and those with cardiovascular disease [1]. Thyroid emergencies are reviewed in the clinical literature [22]. The boxed warning notes that larger doses in euthyroid patients may be life-threatening [1].
